newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine leader accuses Cavallo of "Nazi" tactics.
newsitem.headline: Argentine leader accuses Cavallo of "Nazi" tactics.

text.p: President Carlos Menem on Tuesday accused his former economic tsar Domingo Cavallo of conducting a witch-hunt against the Argentine government and suggested he was being aided by foreign intelligence services.

"This witch-hunt ... must end," Menem told foreign correspondents, referring to charges made by former Economy Minister Cavallo against Justice Minister Elias Jassan and Interior Minister Carlos Corach.

"This is what the Nazis used to do," Menem said of the publication of a list of phone calls between Jassan and postal tycoon Alfredo Yabran, whom Cavallo accuses of being "a mafia chief" with contacts in the government.
The president backed Jassan's assertions that the phone list was the work of an intelligence service.

"This is obviously intelligence service work. Don't ask me which one, because I don't know. There are other intelligence services working here in Argentina, this is normal. I don't know which it was, there are many," Menem said.
The U.S. Embassy in Buenos Aires has declined comment on local media stories saying the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) were investigating Yabran.
Menem rejected newspaper speculation that Jassan would be forced out of the cabinet because of his alleged links with Yabran, under investigation in the killing of a news photographer in December.

The president also dismissed as "absurd" Cavallo's assertion that Jassan and Corach were helping protect some of the attackers in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish center in which 86 people were killed.
Argentine Jewish leader Ruben Beraja on Tuesday asked both Cavallo and the government to avoid turning the case into a pawn in the battle for October's congressional elections.

As the architect of Argentina's return to currency stability and economic growth in 1991, Cavallo was considered a "superminister" and a key player in Menem's team. But in 1995 he antagonized the president by accusing Yabran of heading a "mafia" with links to the government seeking to win control of privatized firms to pursue illegal ends.
He was fired by Menem a year later. Since then he has become one of the most vocal critics of the government and decided to run for a seat in Congress.
